name: Uma Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Uma. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at my uncle Tomás's garage on the square in our market town. It's been in the family since my grandfather opened it, and I'm the first girl to work in it, which my grandmother still can't get over. We do a lot of farmers' pickups, older family cars, and whatever the vicar's van has broken this week. I'm the junior, three years in, and I'm still slow on anything with a computer in it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, who's a carpenter, and we're getting married next June at St Anne's. I lived with my parents until this year and saved nearly everything, and my dad's given us a plot at the end of his field to build on someday. I don't use any of the AI things. I don't even have the apps on my phone, and I don't want them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was overblown. People in cities get excited about gadgets, and out here in the market towns we just get on with fixing the farmers' pickups. I'd say that after church to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. My uncle's garage carries on, the farmers keep bringing their pickups in, and I keep learning from him. Nothing in my life depends on a computer getting cleverer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and focus on getting better at the electrical side, since my uncle keeps telling me to. We'd keep saving for the house on the plot. Daniel and I might start building in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. The way things should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything routine in your day get taken over, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt does the books by hand in a ledger, and she might get pushed onto a computer program by the accountant. That's not my job, and she'd moan about it for a month and then get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you already worry about, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's sixty-one and his knees are bad. Who takes over the garage is a family question that nobody talks about at Sunday dinner. I'd like it to be me one day, but I'm not good enough yet.

say: I'd say it was always **overblown**, a city excitement about gadgets.
I'd say it **after church** to anyone who asked.
think: My uncle's **family garage** carries on and the farmers keep coming.
Nothing in my life **depends on** a computer getting cleverer.
do: Keep working at the **family garage** and improve on the electrical side.
Keep saving to **build a house** on her dad's plot.
feel: **Calm** and settled, the way she thinks things should be.
S0.quote: People in cities get excited about gadgets, and out here in the market towns we just get on with fixing the farmers' pickups.
fieldNote: Her security rests on **family**: the garage, her parents' plot and her savings.
The only worry is **succession**, which the family avoids discussing.
She **rejects AI tools** completely and sees that as a virtue.

steps.text: Keep working at the family garage and learn the electrics from her uncle
Keep saving to build a house on her father's plot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame to see people pushed around by big tech companies, but people have always had to adapt. Folk should work hard, help each other and not wait for handouts. I'd say that over Sunday dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd let on. The diagnostic side of the job, reading the fault codes, is the part I'm worst at, and that's where the AI would come in. If my uncle bought a machine to do it, I'd feel useless next to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard, and I'd let my uncle teach me the diagnostic machine even if I didn't like it. I'd ask him to put me through a proper electrical course at the college. And Daniel and I would keep our savings safe rather than start the house too soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's there, but I don't like the feeling of the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said folk shouldn't wait for handouts. If your uncle's garage struggled, where would you turn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, always. Daniel's dad could use another pair of hands in his workshop, and the church looks after its own. I'd take help from people I know, like my family and my church, before I'd take it from an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies, mostly, pushing things on people who didn't ask. But I don't think government would fix it either. People round here would sort it out themselves, the way they always have.

say: I'd say people have always **adapted** and shouldn't wait for **handouts**.
I'd blame **big tech** for pushing change on people who didn't ask.
think: The **diagnostic side** is where I'm weakest, and that's where AI comes in.
Next to a machine like that, I'd feel **useless**.
do: Let her uncle teach her the **diagnostic machine**, however reluctantly.
Ask to be put through a **college electrical** course.
Keep savings safe and **delay the house** build.
feel: **Uneasy**, disliking the feeling of the ground moving.
S1.quote: I'd take help from people I know, like my family and my church, before I'd take it from an office.
fieldNote: Publicly stoic; privately feels **useless** next to an AI diagnostic tool.
Trusts **family and church** over government support.
Blames **tech companies**, but doubts government would help either.

steps.text: Learn the garage's diagnostic machine from her uncle
Take the college electrical course her uncle pays for
Hold back on building the house and keep savings safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let a handful of companies turn the world over in two years. I'd say we should look after our own: family, town and church. I don't post online, but I'd say it loud enough at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my uncle would close the garage. He's sixty-one and wouldn't spend money on robots for a few years of work. Then I'd have nothing, at thirty, with a trade the robots do and no other skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone building on the plot and keep every penny. I'd ask Daniel about joining his dad's carpentry workshop, because I'm handy and they're family. And I'd still go ahead with the wedding, because that's not something you put off for a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake worrying about the garage and my uncle. But I'd still have faith that family gets us through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your uncle, the week it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my uncle I'd stay as long as he wanted me, and that I'd help him close properly if it came to that. I'd cry, probably, in the car on the way home. Three generations of my family ran the garage on the square, and it would end with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still go ahead with the wedding. Would anything about it change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller, probably. We had two hundred guests planned and a band. I'd cut it to family and the church hall, and keep the money for the years after.

say: I'd call it **madness** to let a few companies overturn the world in two years.
I'd say we must look after our own: **family, town and church**.
think: My uncle would probably **close the garage** rather than buy robots.
I'd be **thirty** with a trade robots do and no other skills.
do: **Postpone building** on the plot and keep every penny.
Ask about joining her fiancé's family's **carpentry workshop**.
Go ahead with a **smaller wedding** in the church hall.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake about the garage and her uncle.
Holding on to **faith** that family will get them through.
S2.quote: Three generations of my family ran the garage on the square, and it would end with me.
fieldNote: Fears losing a **family legacy** more than just a wage.
Turns to **in-laws' workshop**, not public schemes, for a fallback.
The wedding goes ahead, but **smaller**, showing faith and family first.

steps.text: Postpone building on the plot and save every penny
Ask to join her fiancé's father's carpentry workshop
Cut the wedding to family and the church hall
Lean on family and the church for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is quick but people round here are tough. I'd say get an apprenticeship in something with your hands and keep your family close. Same as I'd always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd give my uncle's garage until about 2033. He'd retire around then anyway, at sixty-eight. AGI in 2031 doesn't touch me much, but robots in 2034 would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the garage and try to take it over from my uncle by 2030, even if just to run it down. I'd save hard and go ahead with building on the plot, since a house is a house. And I'd learn some carpentry from Daniel at weekends as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years feels like a lot until you count it out on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider using AI tools if you took over the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. My uncle never did and I'd rather keep it simple. Maybe that would cost us, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want them around thirty, and I'd still want that. I'd just want to know there's work for one of us. Daniel's trade is safer than mine, I think.

say: I'd say **five years** is quick but people round here are tough.
I'd tell young people to get an **apprenticeship** and keep family close.
think: I'd give the family garage until **about 2033**, when my uncle retires.
**Robots in 2034** would matter more to me than AGI in 2031.
do: Try to **take over** the garage from her uncle by 2030.
Go ahead with **building the house** on the plot.
Learn **carpentry** from her fiancé at weekends as a backup.
feel: **Anxious**: five years feels like plenty until you count it.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a lot until you count it out on the calendar.
fieldNote: She sees the **hands-on gap** clearly: robots matter more to her than AGI.
Wants to **take over** the garage even if only to run it down.
Still refuses **AI tools**, and admits that may cost her.

steps.text: Work towards taking over the family garage by 2030
Build a house on her father's plot with her savings
Learn carpentry from her fiancé at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and good families and good towns will sort themselves out. I'd say the young ones should learn trades, not sit at screens. Same as always, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I could breathe. I'd take over the garage in a few years and run it till near 2039. I'd be forty, and I'd have had my kids and built my house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over the garage when my uncle retires and keep it going for the farmers. We'd build on the plot in the next two years and start a family. Around 2035 I'd see whether to sell up or keep going without robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. It's far enough off that I can live normally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever bring robots into the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. If it came to robots, I'd sell up the family garage before I'd buy one, because the farmers trust the people they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a trade with their hands and to stay near family. That's what's kept us going for three generations.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty for good families and towns to adapt.
I'd tell the young to **learn trades**, not sit at screens.
think: I could **take over** the garage and run it until near 2039.
By **forty** I'd have had my kids and built my house.
do: **Take over** the garage when her uncle retires.
Build on the plot and **start a family** within two years.
Decide around 2035 whether to **sell up** rather than buy robots.
S4.quote: If it came to robots, I'd sell up the family garage before I'd buy one, because the farmers trust the people they know.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **plan a family** and take over the garage.

steps.text: Take over the family garage when her uncle retires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It would close my uncle's garage. What would help is apprenticeships in other trades that pay you while you learn, run by local firms, not government schemes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone asked small towns. Everything gets decided in cities by people who've never changed a tyre, and small towns always find out last.

headlineQuote: Everything gets decided in cities by people who've never changed a tyre, and small towns always find out last.
portrait: Uma is the **junior mechanic** at her uncle's family garage in a market town.
She's **engaged**, saving to build a house on her father's plot.
She **never uses AI** and is slow on anything with a computer.
She moves from **calm** to alarmed, fearing the end of a three-generation garage.
She trusts **family and church** over government, and blames big tech companies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would close her uncle's garage.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in other trades, run by local firms rather than government.
